summary: In Greek mythology, Adrastus is the Trojan warrior whom Menelaus captures alive after a chariot wreck; Adrastus begs for ransom, Menelaus is minded to spare him, and Agamemnon overrules his brother and kills the captive. The atlas keeps him distinct from Adrastus son of Merops and from Patroclus' victim, though some commentators conflate the Meropsid with this ransom scene.
etymology: Ancient Greek Ἄδραστος / Ἄδρηστος, perhaps "the inescapable."

sections.heading: Menelaus' captive
paragraphs: In Iliad 6 Adrastus' horses bolt into a tamarisk; he rolls from the chariot, clasps Menelaus' knees, and promises rich ransom from his father's halls. Menelaus is about to take him prisoner when Agamemnon arrives, rebukes any thought of mercy, and persuades his brother; Adrastus springs up to flee and Agamemnon spears him in the back.

Wikipedia notes that Leaf and Parada treat this Adrastus as the same man as Merops' son, while Munn and this atlas keep them distinct — otherwise the Iliad would have both Agamemnon and Diomedes kill the same warrior at different times.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: The atlas id adrastus-trojan-ransom is the Iliad-6 captive alone. Distinct from adrastus (Argive king), adrastus-meropsid (Percotean ally slain by Diomedes), and adrastus-trojan (Patroclus' victim in Iliad 16).
